questions.title: Docker Containers vs Virtual Machines
questions.question: What is Docker and how do containers differ from virtual machines?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Container: process isolation using Linux namespaces and cgroups — shares host kernel
- VM: full OS virtualization — hypervisor emulates hardware, each VM has own kernel
- Container advantages: milliseconds to start, MB in size, low overhead
- VM advantages: stronger isolation, different OS/kernel, better security boundaries
- Docker image: read-only filesystem layers; container: running image instance + writable layer
- Docker Hub / ECR: container registries for storing and distributing images
- Use case: containers for application packaging and deployment; VMs for strong isolation

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Docker containers are process isolation mechanisms — they use Linux kernel features like namespaces and control groups to make a process think it has its own filesystem, network, and process space, while actually sharing the host kernel. Virtual machines emulate entire hardware and run a completely separate kernel. This makes containers dramatically more lightweight: a container starts in milliseconds and uses megabytes, while a VM takes minutes to boot and uses gigabytes.

The tradeoff is isolation strength. Containers share the host kernel, so a kernel vulnerability could theoretically affect all containers on that host. VMs have a hypervisor boundary that provides much stronger isolation. For most web application workloads, container isolation is sufficient. For multi-tenant environments where you're running code from different customers, VMs or stronger container isolation techniques are used.

A Docker image is a stack of read-only filesystem layers built from a Dockerfile. Each instruction creates a new layer. When you run an image as a container, Docker adds a thin writable layer on top. Multiple containers can run from the same image without duplicating the read-only data — they all share the image layers.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Container vs VM Architecture

```
Virtual Machines:
┌──────────────┐  ┌──────────────┐
│  App + Libs  │  │  App + Libs  │
│  Guest OS    │  │  Guest OS    │  (each has full OS — 2-20GB each)
└──────┬───────┘  └──────┬───────┘
       └────────┬─────────┘
          Hypervisor
          Host OS
          Hardware

Docker Containers:
┌────────┐  ┌────────┐  ┌────────┐
│App+Libs│  │App+Libs│  │App+Libs│  (just app + deps — 50-500MB each)
└────┬───┘  └────┬───┘  └────┬───┘
     └───────────┼────────────┘
             Docker Engine
             Host OS Kernel (shared)
             Hardware
```

## Image Layers

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre        # Layer 1: base JRE (~200MB, pulled once)
WORKDIR /app                        # Layer 2: create directory
COPY target/app.jar .               # Layer 3: your JAR (~50MB)
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# Layer 1 is cached and reused across all your Spring Boot images
# Only layer 3 changes on each build → fast rebuilds
```

## Essential Docker Commands

```bash
# Build image
docker build -t my-app:1.0 .
docker build -t my-app:1.0 --no-cache .  # rebuild from scratch

# Run container
docker run -d --name my-app \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod \
  -e DB_HOST=postgres \
  --network my-network \
  my-app:1.0

# Inspect and debug
docker logs my-app -f          # stream logs
docker exec -it my-app /bin/sh  # interactive shell
docker stats my-app             # CPU/memory usage

# Cleanup
docker stop my-app && docker rm my-app
docker image prune -f           # remove unused images
```

questions.title: Writing Optimal Dockerfiles for Java
questions.question: How do you write an optimal Dockerfile for a Spring Boot Java application?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Multi-stage build: builder stage with JDK, final stage with lean JRE
- Layer caching: COPY dependencies before source code — rebuild only changed layers
- Spring Boot layered JAR: explode JAR layers for optimal caching (dependencies rarely change)
- Non-root user: run container as non-root for security
- .dockerignore: exclude target/, .git/, test files from build context
- JVM flags for containers: -XX:+UseContainerSupport, -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0
- Healthcheck in Dockerfile or Docker Compose for container health monitoring

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The two key optimizations for Spring Boot Dockerfiles are multi-stage builds and layered JAR extraction. Multi-stage builds use a full JDK image to compile and package, then copy only the output into a lean JRE image. This makes the final image 3-5 times smaller — no compiler, no Maven, no test dependencies.

Layered JAR extraction takes advantage of Spring Boot's ability to split the JAR into layers based on how frequently they change: snapshot dependencies at the bottom, regular dependencies, Spring Boot loader, application classes at the top. The lower layers rarely change, so Docker caches them. When you push a new version, only the application layer needs to be transferred. This dramatically speeds up deployments in CI/CD.

Always run your container as a non-root user. If a process inside a container is compromised, a non-root user limits the blast radius. Create a dedicated application user in the Dockerfile and switch to it before the ENTRYPOINT.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Optimal Spring Boot Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# ===== Stage 1: Build =====
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /build

# Cache Maven dependencies separately (only re-runs if pom.xml changes)
COPY pom.xml .
COPY .mvn .mvn
COPY mvnw .
RUN ./mvnw dependency:go-offline -q

# Build app
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests -q

# Extract layered JAR for optimal caching
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract --destination /layers

# ===== Stage 2: Runtime =====
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app

# Security: non-root user
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

# Copy layers from least-changed to most-changed (Docker caches lower layers)
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder --chown=appuser:appgroup /layers/application/ ./

USER appuser
EXPOSE 8080

# Container-aware JVM settings
ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseContainerSupport \
               -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
               -XX:+UseG1GC \
               -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom"

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=60s --retries=3 \
    CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```

## .dockerignore

```
# .dockerignore — exclude from build context
target/
.git/
.gitignore
*.md
DOCKERFILE
docker-compose*.yml
.idea/
*.iml
test-results/
```

## Image Size Comparison

```
Without multi-stage (JDK + fat JAR):  ~500MB
With multi-stage (JRE + fat JAR):     ~250MB
With multi-stage + layered JAR:       ~250MB but deploys MUCH faster
→ Only the application layer (~5MB) transferred on code changes
```

speakable_v2.hook: The two key optimizations for Spring Boot Dockerfiles are multi-stage builds and layered JAR extraction.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Create a dedicated application user in the Dockerfile and switch to it before the ENTRYPOINT.

questions.title: Docker Volumes and Networking
questions.question: How do Docker volumes and networking work, and how do containers communicate with each other?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Volume: persists data outside container lifecycle — survives container restarts and removals
- Named volume: managed by Docker, best for databases and persistent data
- Bind mount: mounts host directory — useful for dev hot-reload but not for production
- Networks: bridge (default), host, none
- User-defined bridge network: containers can communicate by container name (DNS resolution)
- Default bridge: containers use IP, no DNS — less useful
- Port mapping: -p hostPort:containerPort
- Container DNS: on user-defined network, container name = hostname

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Docker volumes decouple data from the container lifecycle. A container is ephemeral — when you stop and remove it, the writable layer is gone. Volumes persist data independently, so your database data survives container restarts, updates, and replacements. Named volumes are managed by Docker — you don't need to know where on the host the data is stored.

For container communication, use user-defined bridge networks rather than the default bridge. On a user-defined network, Docker provides automatic DNS resolution — containers can reach each other by their service or container name. If your Spring Boot app and PostgreSQL container are both on the same network, the app can connect to postgres:5432 where postgres is the PostgreSQL container name.

Bind mounts are useful in development — you mount your source code directory into the container and the application sees live changes without rebuilding the image. In production, always use named volumes for persistent data and never bind-mount your entire source tree.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Volumes

```bash
# Named volume — Docker manages location
docker volume create postgres-data

docker run -d \
  --name postgres \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  -v postgres-data:/var/lib/postgresql/data \
  postgres:16-alpine

# Bind mount — mount host directory (dev only)
docker run -d \
  --name spring-dev \
  -v $(pwd)/src:/app/src \
  -v $(pwd)/target:/app/target \
  my-app:dev
```

## Networks

```bash
# Create a user-defined network
docker network create app-network

# Run PostgreSQL on the network
docker run -d \
  --name postgres \
  --network app-network \
  -e POSTGRES_DB=appdb \
  -e POSTGRES_PASSWORD=secret \
  postgres:16-alpine

# Run Spring Boot on same network
docker run -d \
  --name spring-api \
  --network app-network \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL=jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/appdb \
  #                                                ↑ container name = hostname
  -e SPRING_DATASOURCE_PASSWORD=secret \
  my-app:latest

# spring-api can reach postgres by hostname 'postgres'
# No IP addresses needed — Docker DNS handles it
```

## Inspect Container Network

```bash
docker network inspect app-network
# Shows all containers on the network and their IPs

docker exec spring-api ping postgres  # verify connectivity by name
docker exec spring-api wget -qO- http://redis:6379  # test another service
```

speakable_v2.hook: Docker volumes decouple data from the container lifecycle.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: In production, always use named volumes for persistent data and never bind-mount your entire source tree.

questions.title: Docker Security Best Practices
questions.question: What are the key security best practices for running Docker containers in production?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Run as non-root user — always specify USER in Dockerfile
- Read-only filesystem: --read-only flag, tmpfs for temp files
- No sensitive data in image: use runtime env vars or secrets mounts
- Scan images for vulnerabilities: docker scout, trivy, snyk
- Minimal base image: distroless or alpine to reduce attack surface
- Drop capabilities: --cap-drop=ALL, add only needed capabilities
- Secrets: use Docker secrets or secret mounts — not environment variables for sensitive data
- Resource limits: --memory and --cpus prevent resource exhaustion

sections.Title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
The most impactful security improvements for containers are running as a non-root user and using minimal base images. If a container runs as root and an attacker exploits a vulnerability in your application, they have root access inside the container, which can be leveraged to escape to the host. Running as a non-root user dramatically limits what an attacker can do.

Minimal base images reduce the attack surface. Every tool in the image is a potential vector. Alpine-based images have only essential utilities. Distroless images go further — they contain only the runtime and your application, no shell, no package manager. If there's no bash in the container, an attacker who gets code execution can't easily move around.

Never put secrets in Dockerfile or image layers. Docker image history shows every layer, and committing a secret makes it visible to anyone who can pull the image. Use environment variables at runtime for non-sensitive configuration, and Docker secrets or secret mounts for sensitive values.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Secure Dockerfile Practices

```dockerfile
# Use specific version — not 'latest' (reproducible builds)
FROM eclipse-temurin:21.0.3_9-jre-alpine

# Create non-root user before COPY
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup

WORKDIR /app
RUN chown appuser:appgroup /app

COPY --chown=appuser:appgroup target/app.jar .

# Switch to non-root BEFORE ENTRYPOINT
USER appuser

# Don't expose ports >= 1024 to avoid privilege issues
EXPOSE 8080

ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-jar", "app.jar"]

# NEVER:
# ENV DB_PASSWORD=mysecret  ← visible in docker history
# COPY .env .  ← don't copy secrets into image
```

## Runtime Security Flags

```bash
# Minimal capabilities, read-only filesystem, resource limits
docker run -d \
  --name spring-api \
  --user 1001:1001 \
  --read-only \
  --tmpfs /tmp:rw,size=100m,mode=1777 \
  --cap-drop=ALL \
  --cap-add=NET_BIND_SERVICE \
  --security-opt no-new-privileges \
  --memory=512m \
  --cpus=1.0 \
  -p 8080:8080 \
  my-app:latest
```

## Vulnerability Scanning

```bash
# Trivy — free, fast, comprehensive
trivy image my-app:latest

# Docker Scout (built into Docker)
docker scout cves my-app:latest

# GitHub Actions: scan before push
- name: Scan for vulnerabilities
  uses: aquasecurity/trivy-action@master
  with:
    image-ref: my-app:${{ github.sha }}
    severity: 'HIGH,CRITICAL'
    exit-code: '1'  # fail build if critical vulnerabilities found
```

## Environment Variables vs Secrets

```bash
# OK for non-sensitive config
docker run -e SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod ...

# Sensitive data: use --secret or inject at runtime from Secrets Manager
docker run --secret id=db_password,env=DB_PASSWORD ...
# or: read from AWS Secrets Manager at startup (recommended)
```

speakable_v2.hook: The most impactful security improvements for containers are running as a non-root user and using minimal base images.
speakable_v2.cap: Use environment variables at runtime for non-sensitive configuration, and Docker secrets or secret mounts for sensitive values.

questions.title: Docker Resource Limits and JVM Tuning
questions.question: How do you set resource limits for Docker containers running Java/Spring Boot applications?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- --memory: hard container memory limit — OOMKilled if exceeded
- --cpus: fractional CPU limit — 0.5 = half a core
- JVM in containers: before Java 11 didn't respect container limits — used host RAM
- -XX:+UseContainerSupport (default Java 11+): JVM reads cgroup limits from container
- -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0: JVM uses 75% of container memory for heap
- Metaspace: off-heap — doesn't count toward heap but counts toward container memory limit
- OOM: application OOM vs container OOM — understand difference
- G1GC (default Java 9+): good for containers; ZGC for low-latency

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Before Java 11, the JVM didn't understand it was running in a container. It read available RAM from the host OS and sized the heap accordingly — a 512MB container running on a 32GB host would try to use 8GB for the heap, immediately causing the container to be killed for exceeding its memory limit.

From Java 11 onwards, UseContainerSupport is enabled by default. The JVM reads its cgroup memory limit — the container's actual limit — and sizes the heap as a percentage of that. With -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0, a 1GB container gets 768MB for the Java heap, leaving 256MB for off-heap memory: Metaspace, thread stacks, native memory, and OS overhead.

The right pattern is to set the container memory limit, let the JVM auto-size its heap from that limit using MaxRAMPercentage, and monitor both JVM heap usage and total container RSS. If the container is being OOMKilled, either the heap limit is too high for non-heap needs, or the application has a memory leak.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Dockerfile JVM Configuration

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY target/app.jar app.jar

# UseContainerSupport is default in Java 11+
# MaxRAMPercentage: heap = 75% of container memory limit
# MaxMetaspaceSize: cap off-heap class metadata
ENV JAVA_OPTS="\
  -XX:+UseContainerSupport \
  -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 \
  -XX:MaxMetaspaceSize=256m \
  -XX:+UseG1GC \
  -XX:+HeapDumpOnOutOfMemoryError \
  -XX:HeapDumpPath=/tmp/heap-dump.hprof \
  -Djava.security.egd=file:/dev/./urandom"

EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS -jar app.jar"]
```

## docker run / Compose Resource Limits

```bash
# docker run
docker run \
  --memory=1g \
  --memory-swap=1g \
  --cpus=0.5 \
  my-spring-app
# --memory: 1GB RAM limit
# --memory-swap = --memory: no swap (swap = 0)
# --cpus=0.5: 50% of one CPU
```

```yaml
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  app:
    image: my-spring-app
    deploy:
      resources:
        limits:
          memory: 1G
          cpus: '0.5'
        reservations:
          memory: 512M
          cpus: '0.25'
```

## Memory Budget Calculation

```
Container memory limit: 1024 MB

JVM Heap (MaxRAMPercentage=75%)  =  768 MB
Metaspace (MaxMetaspaceSize)     =  256 MB
Thread stacks (200 threads×1MB)  =  200 MB
CodeCache                        =   64 MB
OS/libc overhead                 =   64 MB
                                 ----------
Total needed                     = 1352 MB  ← EXCEEDS 1024MB!

Fix: increase container to 1.5GB, or
     reduce MaxRAMPercentage to 60%:
     768MB × 0.6 = 460MB heap
     460 + 256 + 200 + 64 + 64 = 1044MB ≈ fits in 1GB
```

speakable_v2.hook: Before Java 11, the JVM didn't understand it was running in a container.

questions.title: Multi-Stage Docker Builds for Java
questions.question: How do you optimize Docker image size and build speed for Spring Boot applications using multi-stage builds?

sections.title: What the Interviewer Wants to Hear
sections.content:
- Multi-stage build: separate build environment from runtime image — smaller, more secure final image
- JDK in build stage, JRE in runtime stage — JDK ~500MB → JRE ~200MB → JRE Alpine ~85MB
- Layer caching: COPY pom.xml + RUN mvn dependency:go-offline BEFORE COPY src — cache deps layer
- Spring Boot layered JAR: extract layers for better cache reuse
- .dockerignore: exclude target/, .git/, *.md — faster context transfer
- BuildKit: parallel stage building, improved cache
- Distroless images: minimal attack surface — no shell, no package manager

sections.title: Interview Answer
sections.content:
Multi-stage builds are essential for Java because the build environment needs the full JDK and Maven or Gradle, but the runtime environment only needs the JRE to execute the compiled JAR. The final image has no source code, no build tools, no Maven cache — only the minimal runtime and the application JAR.

Layer caching is the key to fast builds in CI. Docker caches each layer and only rebuilds from the point where something changed. The critical optimization is separating dependency download from source compilation. Copy pom.xml and run mvn dependency:go-offline before copying source code. Dependencies change rarely; source code changes every commit. This way, dependency download is cached and skipped unless pom.xml changes.

Spring Boot 2.3+ introduced layered JARs. Instead of one fat JAR, the application is split into layers by how often they change: dependencies (rarely), Spring Boot itself (occasionally), your application code (frequently). Each layer becomes a Docker layer, maximizing cache reuse when only code changes.

sections.title: Concept Explained
sections.content:
## Optimized Multi-Stage Dockerfile

```dockerfile
# Stage 1: Build — uses full JDK + Maven
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app

# Copy ONLY dependency files first — cache this layer
COPY pom.xml .
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY mvnw .
RUN chmod +x mvnw && ./mvnw dependency:go-offline -q
# ^ This layer is cached unless pom.xml changes

# Now copy source — this invalidates cache only when code changes
COPY src ./src
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests -q

# Extract Spring Boot layers
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract

# Stage 2: Runtime — uses minimal JRE
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine AS runtime
WORKDIR /app

# Non-root user for security
RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
USER appuser

# Copy Spring Boot layers in order (slowest to fastest changing)
# Each COPY = Docker layer = individual caching
COPY --from=builder /app/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/application/ ./

ENV JAVA_OPTS="-XX:+UseContainerSupport -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0"
EXPOSE 8080

HEALTHCHECK --interval=30s --timeout=5s --start-period=60s --retries=3 \
  CMD wget -qO- http://localhost:8080/actuator/health || exit 1

ENTRYPOINT ["sh", "-c", "java $JAVA_OPTS org.springframework.boot.loader.JarLauncher"]
```

## .dockerignore

```
target/
.git/
.gitignore
*.md
.mvn/wrapper/maven-wrapper.jar
docker-compose*.yml
**/*.log
.env
```

## Image Size Comparison

```
No optimization (fat JAR on JDK image):   ~600 MB
Multi-stage, JRE Alpine, no layers:       ~200 MB
Multi-stage, JRE Alpine, Spring layers:   ~200 MB (but better layer cache)
Distroless JRE:                           ~130 MB

Spring Boot layered build cache hit:
  Without layers: rebuild + push ~120MB JAR every commit
  With layers: only app layer (~5MB) pushed when only code changes
```

speakable_v2.hook: Multi-stage builds are essential for Java because the build environment needs the full JDK and Maven or Gradle, but the runtime environment only needs the JRE to execute the compiled JAR.

beats.text: The production failure mode here is unchecked state mutation under concurrent access.

speakable_v2.cap: Each layer becomes a Docker layer, maximizing cache reuse when only code changes.

questions.question: How do you write an optimized multi-stage Dockerfile for a Spring Boot application?
questions.title: Multi-Stage Dockerfile for Spring Boot: Smaller, Faster Images
questions.direct_answer: Use a multi-stage Dockerfile: stage 1 uses a JDK image to build the JAR with Maven/Gradle, stage 2 uses a minimal JRE image (eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine) to run only the extracted layers. This reduces image size from 500MB+ to ~150MB by excluding build tools and keeping only runtime dependencies.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Docker image optimization techniques and understand why large images are a problem in CI/CD pipelines
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using a JDK image in the final stage (includes compiler, tools not needed at runtime) or copying the fat JAR without layer splitting
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain Spring Boot's layered JAR format (application code changes more often than dependencies), show COPY --from=builder for selective artifact copying, and mention .dockerignore

sections.title: Why a 500MB Image Slows Your Entire Release Pipeline
sections.content:
Shipping a Spring Boot application to production used to mean pushing 500MB images through CI/CD pipelines — images packed with the Java compiler, Maven wrappers, downloaded dependencies, and your actual application code buried somewhere inside. Every deployment pulled hundreds of megabytes of tools that would never execute in production, wasting bandwidth and slowing rollout.

**Multi-stage builds** fix this by splitting one Dockerfile into two environments: a builder stage with the full JDK that compiles the application, and a runtime stage with only a slim JRE that runs the compiled artifact. The builder stage is discarded entirely — the final image contains nothing from it except the specific files you explicitly copy out.

But image size is only half the story. Spring Boot's **layered JAR format** adds a second optimization that dramatically improves rebuild speed. It splits the fat JAR into four layers ordered by change frequency, so Docker caches the 200MB dependency layer across builds and only transfers the 2MB application layer when code changes. Without layer extraction, every code change forces a full image push even though 98% of the content is unchanged.

sections.title: Separate Dependency Downloads from Source Compilation
sections.content:
The builder stage starts from a full JDK image because Maven needs the Java compiler. The critical optimization is copying the build descriptor before the source code — this creates two distinct cache layers with very different invalidation rates.

When you change a Java source file, Docker detects that `COPY src/` invalidates the cache at that layer. But the earlier `pom.xml` layer and the **dependency download** remain cached because their inputs have not changed. Without this separation, a single `COPY . .` invalidates everything on any file change, triggering a multi-minute dependency re-download on every build.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jdk-alpine AS builder
WORKDIR /app
COPY pom.xml .
COPY .mvn/ .mvn/
COPY mvnw .
RUN ./mvnw dependency:go-offline -B
COPY src/ src/
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests -B
RUN java -Djarmode=layertools -jar target/*.jar extract --destination extracted
```

The final `extract` command unpacks the fat JAR into four directories: `dependencies`, `spring-boot-loader`, `snapshot-dependencies`, and `application`. Each directory becomes a separate Docker layer in the runtime stage, ordered from least to most frequently changing.

sections.title: Build a Runtime Image That Ships Only What Runs
sections.content:
The runtime stage starts from `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` — roughly 80MB compared to the builder's 400MB+ because it excludes the compiler, Maven, and all source code. The **COPY order** from the extracted layers mirrors change frequency and directly controls cache efficiency.

Dependencies change only when `pom.xml` changes, which might happen weekly. The Spring Boot loader changes only during framework upgrades. Application code changes with every commit. Copying in this order means most builds invalidate and re-push only the final application layer.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
WORKDIR /app
COPY --from=builder /app/extracted/dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/extracted/spring-boot-loader/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/extracted/snapshot-dependencies/ ./
COPY --from=builder /app/extracted/application/ ./
RUN addgroup -S spring && adduser -S spring -G spring
USER spring
EXPOSE 8080
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "org.springframework.boot.loader.launch.JarLauncher"]
```

Running as a **non-root user** is essential for production images. The `adduser` command creates a system user with no home directory and no login shell. If an attacker exploits a vulnerability in your application, they gain only the limited permissions of this unprivileged user rather than root access to the container filesystem.

sections.title: The Build Context Trap That Silently Slows Every Build
sections.content:
Without a `.dockerignore` file, Docker sends the entire project directory as the build context — including `.git/` history, `target/` output, IDE configuration, and any local data files. On a project with a populated `target/` directory, this can add hundreds of megabytes to the context transfer before a single instruction executes.

The fix is a minimal `.dockerignore` that excludes everything the build does not need.

```
target/
.git/
.idea/
*.iml
*.md
.env
node_modules/
```

**JVM tuning flags** like `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` belong in your Kubernetes deployment manifest or `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` environment variable, not hardcoded in the Dockerfile. Baking JVM flags into the image means rebuilding and redeploying every time you need to adjust memory settings — exactly the kind of unnecessary coupling that containers are designed to eliminate. Set memory and GC flags per environment through orchestration configuration so the same image runs in dev, staging, and production with different tuning.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Multi-stage builds discard the entire build environment** — the JDK, Maven, source code, and downloaded internet never ship to production, cutting image size from 500MB+ to ~150MB and reducing attack surface
- **Layered JAR extraction separates dependencies from application code** — `java -Djarmode=layertools` splits into four layers so Docker reuses the stable 200MB dependency layer and only rebuilds the 2MB application layer on code changes
- **COPY order determines cache behavior** — copy `pom.xml` and run `dependency:go-offline` before `COPY src/` so routine code edits never invalidate the expensive dependency download layer
- **`.dockerignore` prevents build context bloat** — excluding `target/`, `.git/`, and IDE files keeps the context transfer fast and stops irrelevant file changes from busting COPY cache
- **JVM flags belong in deployment manifests, not Dockerfiles** — `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` or Kubernetes env vars let you tune `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage` per environment without rebuilding the image

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
A multi-stage Dockerfile builds your application in one Docker image and then copies only the compiled output into a minimal second image. The result: a production image that has no JDK, no Maven binary, and no source code — just the JRE and the artifact.

**Stage 1 — build stage**
- The build stage uses a full JDK image (e.g., `eclipse-temurin:21-jdk`) with Maven or Gradle; you copy the POM and download dependencies first, before copying source files — Docker caches the dependency layer and only re-downloads when the POM changes
- A common optimization: `COPY pom.xml .` then `RUN mvn dependency:go-offline` before `COPY src ./src` — a code-only change hits the cached dependency layer and the build skips the download phase entirely
- The build stage image grows to 400–600 MB with all build tooling included — it never reaches production; only the `FROM scratch` or minimal second stage does

**Stage 2 — runtime stage**
- Use a JRE-only image for the runtime stage (e.g., `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine`), which is 60–80 MB versus 200+ MB for the full JDK — a smaller image means faster pulls, a smaller attack surface, and less container startup time
- `COPY --from=build /app/target/app.jar /app/app.jar` copies only the JAR from the build stage; the entire Maven cache, source tree, and JDK binaries never enter the final image
- For Spring Boot, enable layered JARs in `pom.xml` and extract layers in the Dockerfile — Spring Boot splits the JAR into dependency, Spring Boot loader, and application layers; Docker caches the stable layers and rebuilds only the application layer on code changes

**Security and production hardening**
- Add `USER appuser` in the runtime stage to run the JVM as a non-root user — a container compromise escalates less far if the process does not have root inside the container
- Pin the base image to a specific digest in production, not just a tag — `eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine` can change when a new Alpine version ships; pinning the digest guarantees reproducibility

questions.direct_answer: Docker caches each instruction's result as a layer. A cache miss invalidates all subsequent layers. Optimize by ordering instructions from least-to-most frequently changing: COPY pom.xml first and run dependency download, then COPY src/ last. This ensures dependency layers are reused across most builds, and only source code layers rebuild on code changes.

sections.title: The One Rule That Makes Docker Builds Fast or Painfully Slow
sections.content:
Most developers blame Docker for slow builds, but the bottleneck is almost always instruction ordering. Docker caches each Dockerfile instruction's result as an immutable layer. Before executing an instruction, Docker checks whether the instruction and its inputs match an existing cached layer. If they match, Docker skips execution entirely and reuses the cached result. If they don't — a **cache miss** — Docker executes that instruction and every instruction after it, even if those later instructions have not changed at all.

This cascade is the single most important concept in Docker performance. A `COPY . .` instruction early in the Dockerfile means any change to any file — a README edit, a test tweak, a `.gitignore` update — invalidates the cache at that layer and forces everything below it to re-execute. For a Java project, "everything below" includes the multi-minute Maven dependency download.

The fix is structural: treat your Dockerfile as a dependency graph. Stable inputs — base images, build descriptors, dependency downloads — belong at the top. Volatile inputs — source code, configuration files, assets — belong at the bottom. This ordering maximizes cache reuse across builds and can cut typical Java build times from seven minutes to under one.

sections.title: How Docker Validates Each Layer's Cache
sections.content:
When Docker encounters a `COPY` or `ADD` instruction, it computes **checksums** of every file being copied and compares them against the checksums stored in the cached layer. A single changed byte in any file triggers a cache miss. For `RUN` instructions, Docker compares the exact command string — if the string is identical and the previous layer was cached, the `RUN` result is reused without execution.

This checksum-based validation explains why `COPY . .` is destructive to performance. Docker checksums every file in the build context. If your `.git/` directory is included (no `.dockerignore`), even a new commit changes file timestamps and metadata, invalidating the cache.

The optimized pattern for Java projects copies only the build descriptor first, then downloads dependencies, then copies source code separately. Each step creates a distinct layer with its own cache key.

```dockerfile
COPY pom.xml .
RUN ./mvnw dependency:go-offline -B
COPY src/ src/
RUN ./mvnw package -DskipTests -B
```

With this ordering, a source code change only invalidates the `COPY src/` layer and the `package` command. The dependency download layer — often the slowest step — stays cached because `pom.xml` has not changed.

sections.title: Why One Changed File Triggers a Full Rebuild — the Invalidation Cascade
sections.content:
The cascade behavior is not obvious until you trace through a real example. Consider a Dockerfile with five instructions: `FROM`, `COPY . .`, `RUN mvn dependency:go-offline`, `COPY src/ src/`, `RUN mvn package`. With `COPY . .` at line 2, changing any Java file invalidates layer 2. Docker must then re-execute layers 3, 4, and 5 — even though the dependency download at layer 3 produces identical output.

**Docker cannot skip ahead to reuse later layers** after a miss. The cache model is strictly linear: if layer N misses, layers N+1 through the end all miss. This is why instruction ordering is not a minor optimization — it is the difference between a 30-second rebuild and a 7-minute rebuild on every code change.

A subtler trap involves `ARG` instructions. Build arguments declared before `FROM` can invalidate the base image selection. Arguments declared after `FROM` but before `RUN` change the cache key for that `RUN` instruction. Passing a CI build number as an `ARG` before your dependency download step forces a full re-download on every CI build, even though the dependencies have not changed. Place volatile `ARG` values as late as possible in the Dockerfile.

sections.title: BuildKit Cache Mounts — Warm Dependencies Even on Cold Builds
sections.content:
BuildKit, Docker's modern builder backend enabled by default since Docker Desktop 23, introduces **cache mounts** that persist package manager caches on the host filesystem without including them in image layers. For Maven projects, mounting `~/.m2/repository` means even a build with no layer cache starts with a warm dependency cache rather than downloading everything from scratch.

```dockerfile
# syntax=docker/dockerfile:1
RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2 \
    ./mvnw package -DskipTests -B
```

Unlike layer caching, which requires identical inputs to produce a hit, cache mounts provide a persistent directory that accumulates artifacts across builds. A new dependency in `pom.xml` triggers a layer cache miss, but the cache mount still contains every previously downloaded JAR — only the new dependency downloads.

BuildKit also runs **independent stages in parallel**. If your Dockerfile has a builder stage and a separate test-runner stage starting from the same base, BuildKit executes both concurrently. In CI environments, pair cache mounts with GitHub Actions' `docker/build-push-action` using `cache-from` and `cache-to` to share layer caches across CI runs. Without this, each CI run starts cold and negates careful instruction ordering.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Cache miss cascades to all later layers** — a single changed file checksum at layer N forces re-execution of layers N+1 through the end, even if those layers would produce identical output
- **`COPY . .` early is the classic Java build killer** — any project file change triggers a full Maven dependency re-download because the broad COPY invalidates the dependency layer
- **`RUN --mount=type=cache,target=/root/.m2`** — BuildKit keeps the Maven local repository on the host between builds without bloating the final image, giving warm cache even on layer misses
- **`ARG` placement matters for cache keys** — a CI build number passed as an ARG before the dependency step forces a full re-download on every build; place volatile ARGs as late as possible
- **BuildKit runs independent stages in parallel** — a builder and a test-runner stage starting from the same base image execute concurrently, shaving minutes off multi-target CI pipelines

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Docker builds images by executing instructions one at a time and caching each resulting layer. The critical rule: Docker invalidates every layer after the first change it detects — instruction order determines whether you get a cache hit or a full rebuild.

**The ordering rule — dependencies before source code**
- Copy and install dependencies before copying source code — `COPY pom.xml .` then `RUN mvn dependency:go-offline`, then `COPY src ./src` ensures a code-only change hits the cached dependency layer and skips the 3-minute download phase
- Once any layer is invalidated, every subsequent layer rebuilds even if its content did not change — a source copy instruction placed before `RUN mvn dependency:go-offline` means every code commit triggers a full dependency re-download
- For Node.js or Python: `COPY package.json .` then `RUN npm install` before `COPY . .` follows the same logic

**`RUN` instruction consolidation**
- Multiple `RUN` instructions each create a separate layer; combining cleanup in the same `RUN` that installs packages keeps the image smaller — `RUN apt-get update && apt-get install -y curl && rm -rf /var/lib/apt/lists/*` in one instruction prevents the package cache from persisting in an intermediate layer
- Splitting an `apt-get update` from `apt-get install` across two `RUN` instructions causes the stale cache problem: Docker caches the update layer and uses the cached package list, then installs potentially outdated packages on the next build
- Don't consolidate instructions that change frequently with instructions that change rarely — a `RUN` that sets up the OS and installs your application JAR will both re-execute on every JAR change

**BuildKit and remote caching**
- Enable BuildKit with `DOCKER_BUILDKIT=1` or use `docker buildx build` — BuildKit parallelizes independent build stages and provides more granular cache invalidation than the classic builder
- `--cache-from` pulls a previous build's layers from a registry for use as cache — CI agents without a local build cache can still achieve cache hits by pulling the most recent image from the registry before building

questions.question: What are the differences between Docker bridge, host, and overlay networking modes?
questions.title: Docker Networking: Bridge vs Host vs Overlay
questions.direct_answer: Bridge network (default) creates an isolated virtual network per host; containers communicate via container names. Host network removes network isolation — container shares the host network stack directly. Overlay network spans multiple Docker hosts (Swarm/Kubernetes) enabling cross-node container communication. Most Spring Boot apps use bridge locally and overlay (via CNI) in Kubernetes.

sections.title: The Port-Mapping Mistake That Reveals a Networking Misunderstanding
sections.content:
The most common Docker networking error in Spring Boot projects is adding `-p 5432:5432` so the app container can talk to the PostgreSQL container — then wondering why the connection uses `localhost`. Containers on the same Docker network reach each other by **service name**, not by published ports. Publishing a port exposes it to the host machine and the outside world, which is exactly what you do not want for internal database traffic.

This misunderstanding stems from conflating two different communication paths: **east-west traffic** (container to container on the same network) and **north-south traffic** (external client to container). Bridge networking handles east-west traffic through Docker's built-in DNS resolver. Host networking removes the network boundary entirely. Overlay networking extends east-west communication across multiple physical machines.

Each mode solves a different problem, and choosing the wrong one creates either unnecessary exposure, performance overhead, or communication failures. The decision framework is straightforward once you understand what each mode actually does to the network stack.

sections.title: Bridge vs Host vs Overlay — What Each Mode Actually Changes
sections.content:
The three modes differ in isolation, DNS behavior, and scope. Understanding these differences prevents the port-mapping mistake and clarifies when each mode is appropriate.

| Dimension | Bridge | Host | Overlay |
|---|---|---|---|
| Network isolation | Isolated virtual network per host | None — shares host network stack | Isolated virtual network across hosts |
| Container DNS | Service name resolves automatically | Uses host DNS, no container names | Service name resolves across nodes |
| Port mapping needed | Only for external access (`-p`) | Not needed — binds directly to host | Via ingress routing or service mesh |
| Performance | Good — minimal NAT overhead | Best — zero NAT, zero bridge | VXLAN encapsulation adds ~5% overhead |
| Multi-host support | Single host only | Single host only | Spans multiple Docker hosts |
| Security surface | Containers isolated from host | Container ports exposed on host directly | Encrypted tunnels between nodes |
| Kubernetes equivalent | Pod-internal network | `hostNetwork: true` | CNI plugin (Calico, Flannel, Cilium) |

Docker Compose automatically creates a **user-defined bridge network** for each project. Every service in the compose file joins this network and can reach every other service by its service name. This is why `jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/myapp` works without any port configuration — Docker's embedded DNS resolves `postgres` to the container's internal IP.

sections.title: Matching the Network Mode to Your Deployment Model
sections.content:
For **local development** with Docker Compose, the default bridge network handles everything. Your Spring Boot app connects to PostgreSQL using the service name `postgres`, and Redis using `redis`. Port mappings with `-p` should only appear when you need host access — for example, exposing `5432` so DBeaver on your laptop can query the database directly.

A common compose setup illustrates this — the app reaches postgres by service name without any published ports between containers, and only the app port is exposed to the host.

```yaml
services:
  app:
    image: my-spring-app
    ports:
      - "8080:8080"
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    # No ports needed for app-to-postgres communication
```

**Host networking** removes all isolation — the container's processes bind directly to the host's network interfaces. The performance benefit is measurable for high-throughput workloads like Kafka brokers or network monitoring tools where even bridge NAT overhead matters. But it sacrifices isolation and risks port conflicts with host services, so use it only when benchmarks justify it.

**Overlay networking** spans multiple Docker hosts using VXLAN tunneling and is the foundation of Docker Swarm's multi-node communication. In practice, if you deploy on Kubernetes — which most production Java teams do — the CNI plugin handles overlay networking transparently. You configure Services and NetworkPolicies rather than managing overlay networks directly. Understanding overlay concepts still matters because the same DNS resolution and network segmentation principles apply in both Swarm and Kubernetes.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Service names are DNS entries on bridge networks** — Docker Compose containers reach each other at `postgres:5432` or `redis:6379` without port mapping, because Docker's embedded DNS resolves service names to container IPs
- **Port mapping (`-p`) is for north-south traffic only** — publishing ports exposes them to the host and external clients; container-to-container communication never needs it and adding it creates unnecessary attack surface
- **Host networking removes all isolation for zero NAT** — the container binds directly to host interfaces, giving best performance but risking port collisions and eliminating network-level security boundaries
- **Overlay uses VXLAN tunneling across hosts** — adds roughly 5% overhead from encapsulation but enables cross-node communication in Docker Swarm; Kubernetes CNI plugins provide the production equivalent
- **User-defined bridge networks outperform the default bridge** — the default `bridge` network lacks automatic DNS resolution; docker-compose creates user-defined networks with DNS built in, which is why service-name connectivity works out of the box

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Docker provides three main network drivers, and choosing the wrong one is the most common reason containers cannot communicate or performance is unexpectedly poor.

**Bridge — the default for single-host communication**
- Every Docker installation creates a default `bridge` network; containers on the same bridge can reach each other by IP, but not by name — user-defined bridge networks enable DNS-based service discovery, which is why you should always create a named bridge and never rely on the default
- Create a user-defined bridge with `docker network create app-network`; containers on it resolve each other by container name — `http://postgres:5432` works from a Spring Boot container if both containers join the same named bridge
- The default bridge network requires you to use `--link` (deprecated) for name resolution, which is why Docker Compose creates a project-specific network by default

**Host — for performance-sensitive workloads**
- `--network host` removes the network namespace boundary; the container uses the host's network stack directly — no NAT, no port mapping overhead, but the container shares the host's IP and port space
- A container on host networking binds ports directly on the host; two containers cannot both bind port 8080 on the same host network
- Appropriate for high-throughput, latency-sensitive workloads where NAT overhead is measurable — avoid it for most application containers because it reduces isolation

**Overlay — for multi-host communication**
- Overlay networks span multiple Docker hosts using VXLAN encapsulation; they are the foundation of Docker Swarm and Kubernetes pod networking
- Services on a Swarm overlay network communicate using the service name as hostname across any node in the cluster — the routing mesh handles which container on which host receives the request
- A misconfigured overlay is usually a firewall rule issue: UDP port 4789 (VXLAN) and TCP port 7946 (control plane) must be open between all nodes

sections.title: The Race Condition Hiding in Every depends_on Without Health Checks
sections.content:
Every team that adopts Docker Compose for local development eventually hits the same confusing failure: Spring Boot starts, tries to connect to PostgreSQL, and gets "connection refused" — even though `depends_on: postgres` is set in the compose file. The problem is that `depends_on` only waits for the container process to start, not for PostgreSQL to finish initializing and accept connections.

On a fast machine, PostgreSQL initializes in two seconds and the race is invisible. On a slower laptop or during first-time setup when PostgreSQL creates its data directory, initialization takes ten to fifteen seconds. Spring Boot's connection pool opens during that window and fails because the database is not ready yet.

The fix is **`condition: service_healthy`** combined with a health check on the PostgreSQL service. Docker polls `pg_isready` at a configured interval, and `depends_on` with the health condition blocks the app container until the health check passes. This eliminates the race condition entirely and makes the compose setup reliable on any machine regardless of hardware speed.

sections.title: Health Checks Turn Startup Order Into Startup Readiness
sections.content:
The compose file below defines PostgreSQL and Redis with health checks, and the Spring Boot app waits for both to be healthy before starting. The **health check commands** verify actual readiness — `pg_isready` confirms PostgreSQL accepts connections, and `redis-cli ping` confirms Redis responds to commands.

The `interval` parameter controls how frequently Docker runs the health check command, while `retries` determines how many consecutive failures mark the container as unhealthy. Setting `interval: 5s` with `retries: 5` means Docker waits up to 25 seconds for the service to become healthy before giving up.

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16-alpine
    environment:
      POSTGRES_DB: myapp
      POSTGRES_USER: user
      POSTGRES_PASSWORD: password
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
    healthcheck:

      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

    healthcheck:
      test: ["CMD", "redis-cli", "ping"]
      interval: 5s
      retries: 5

    build: .

Without it, every restart wipes the database and you lose all test data and schema migrations. Use `docker compose down -v` only when you intentionally want a clean slate — for example, when resetting a corrupted development database.

sections.title: Profiles Let You Run Databases Without Rebuilding the App Image
sections.content:
During active development, rebuilding the Docker image on every code change is slow compared to running the Spring Boot app directly from your IDE with hot reload. **Compose profiles** solve this by letting you start only the infrastructure containers while developing the application locally.

The profile configuration assigns each service to one or more named profiles, giving you flexible startup control.

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    profiles: ["infra", "full"]
    # ...config as above
  redis:
    profiles: ["infra", "full"]
    # ...config as above
  app:
    profiles: ["full"]
    # ...config as above
```

With `docker compose --profile infra up -d`, only PostgreSQL and Redis start. Your IDE runs the Spring Boot app with `application-local.yml` pointing to `localhost:5432` and `localhost:6379`. When you need the full stack — for integration testing or demoing — `docker compose --profile full up` starts everything including the app container.

This workflow eliminates the most common developer complaint about Docker Compose: the slow image rebuild cycle. Infrastructure runs in containers for consistency, the application runs natively for speed. The **service DNS names** (`postgres`, `redis`) work identically whether the app is inside or outside Docker — the only change is the hostname in configuration, which Spring profiles handle cleanly.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`depends_on` alone is a race condition** — it waits for container start, not service readiness; `condition: service_healthy` with `pg_isready` and `redis-cli ping` blocks until dependencies actually accept connections
- **Service names are DNS hostnames** — `jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/myapp` works because Docker's built-in DNS resolves `postgres` to the container's IP on the shared bridge network
- **Named volumes persist data across restarts** — `postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data` survives `docker compose down` so you keep schema and test data; only `down -v` wipes it
- **Profiles separate infrastructure from application** — `--profile infra` starts only databases so developers can run Spring Boot from the IDE with hot reload, avoiding slow image rebuilds
- **Environment variables override Spring config inside compose** — `SPRING_DATASOURCE_URL` maps to `spring.datasource.url` automatically, letting one compose file serve both container and IDE workflows

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Docker Compose lets you define a multi-container application as a single YAML file and manage the entire stack with one command. For local development, it replaces running three separate Docker commands and manually creating networks.

**Service definition and networking**
- Each service in `docker-compose.yml` maps to one container; Compose creates a project-specific bridge network automatically — services resolve each other by name, so your Spring Boot app connects to `jdbc:postgresql://postgres:5432/mydb` by the service name `postgres`, not by IP
- The `depends_on` directive controls startup order but not readiness — `depends_on: [postgres]` ensures the Postgres container starts before Spring Boot, but Postgres is not necessarily accepting connections yet; add a `healthcheck` to the postgres service and use `condition: service_healthy` to wait for actual readiness
- Without health check conditions, Spring Boot starts before Postgres is ready and fails with connection refused — the most common first-time Docker Compose debugging problem

**Environment variables and secrets**
- Define credentials in a `.env` file and reference them as `${POSTGRES_PASSWORD}` in the YAML — Compose reads `.env` automatically and substitutes values; never hardcode passwords directly in the YAML
- Add `.env` to `.gitignore` immediately — it is the most common way credentials leak into public repositories; commit a `.env.example` with placeholder values instead
- Production does not use Docker Compose; secrets in production go through the orchestrator's secret management (Kubernetes Secrets, AWS Secrets Manager) — Docker Compose is for local development and integration testing

**Volume persistence**
- Named volumes (`volumes: postgres_data: {}`) survive `docker compose down`; bind mounts do not — use named volumes for database data directories so a development database is not lost on every stack restart
- `docker compose down -v` removes named volumes explicitly — useful when you need a clean database state, but easy to confuse with bare `docker compose down` which keeps the data

questions.question: How do JVM memory settings interact with Docker container memory limits, and what can go wrong?
questions.title: JVM Memory in Docker: -Xmx vs Container Limits and OOMKilled
questions.direct_answer: Before JDK 11, the JVM didn't respect cgroup memory limits — it sized the heap based on total host RAM, causing OOMKilled when the container exceeded its limit. JDK 11+ with -XX:+UseContainerSupport (default) reads the cgroup limit correctly. Use -XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0 instead of fixed -Xmx to size heap as a percentage of container memory.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of JVM memory model inside containers and the common OOMKilled production incident
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Setting -Xmx to the container limit (e.g., -Xmx512m in a 512m container) — the JVM needs memory beyond heap for metaspace, threads, code cache, GC overhead
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the difference between heap and non-heap JVM memory, why MaxRAMPercentage of 75% is the standard recommendation, and how to use kubectl describe pod to diagnose OOMKilled

sections.title: The OOMKilled Loop That Hits Every Java Team Moving to Kubernetes
sections.content:
The scenario repeats across every Java team adopting Kubernetes: a Spring Boot application runs fine on a developer's laptop with 16GB RAM, gets deployed to a container with a 512Mi memory limit, and enters an **OOMKilled restart loop**. The pod starts, runs for a few minutes under load, then Kubernetes kills it with exit code 137. The pod restarts and the cycle repeats.

The instinctive fix — setting `-Xmx512m` to match the container limit — makes the problem worse, not better. The JVM heap is only one component of the memory a Java process consumes. Metaspace holds loaded class metadata and can reach 150MB in a Spring Boot application with Hibernate, Jackson, and Spring's proxy infrastructure. Each thread stack occupies about 1MB by default, and Tomcat's thread pool alone can claim 200MB. JIT-compiled code cache, GC overhead, and NIO direct buffers add more.

The total resident memory of a JVM routinely exceeds the heap by 200-400MB. Setting `-Xmx` equal to the container limit guarantees that the process exceeds the cgroup memory ceiling — the kernel's OOM killer terminates it without warning.

sections.title: The Configuration That Guarantees OOMKilled Under Load
sections.content:
The broken configuration sets the JVM heap to the full container memory limit, leaving zero room for non-heap memory regions. This works during light testing because the heap is not fully utilized, but fails under production-like load when the heap fills and non-heap regions grow.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
ENTRYPOINT ["java", "-Xmx512m", "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

Paired with a Kubernetes deployment that sets the same value as the container limit, this creates a guaranteed failure.

```yaml
resources:
  limits:
    memory: 512Mi
```

The JVM allocates up to 512MB for heap objects. But a typical Spring Boot application also consumes 100-150MB for metaspace, 50-200MB for thread stacks depending on pool sizes, 50-100MB for JIT code cache, and additional memory for GC bookkeeping and direct byte buffers. The total **resident set size** (RSS) reaches 700-900MB — far exceeding the 512Mi container limit.

sections.title: Tracing the Kill Signal from Kubernetes Back to the Kernel
sections.content:
When a container exceeds its memory limit, the Linux kernel's **OOM killer** sends SIGKILL (signal 9) to the process. Kubernetes detects the abnormal exit and reports it as OOMKilled in the pod status. The diagnosis starts with `kubectl describe pod` which shows the termination reason and the exit code.

The JVM itself never reports an OutOfMemoryError in this scenario because the kill comes from outside the process. The kernel terminates the process before the JVM's own memory management can react. This is why application logs often show nothing unusual before the crash — the last log line is a normal request, then silence.

To confirm the diagnosis, check `kubectl describe pod <name>` for `OOMKilled` in the last state, and `kubectl top pod` for real-time memory usage approaching the limit. On the node, `dmesg` shows the kernel's kill decision with the exact RSS that triggered it.

The **memory breakdown** for a typical Spring Boot app in a 512Mi container reveals the problem clearly: heap should be around 350-380MB (75% of 512), but metaspace needs 100-150MB, thread stacks need 50-100MB, and code cache needs another 50MB. The sum exceeds 512Mi even with a conservatively sized heap.

sections.title: MaxRAMPercentage Sizes the Heap Relative to the Container Limit
sections.content:
The correct approach uses `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` instead of a fixed `-Xmx` value. This tells the JVM to size its maximum heap as 75% of the detected container memory limit, leaving 25% headroom for all non-heap memory regions.

```dockerfile
FROM eclipse-temurin:21-jre-alpine
ENTRYPOINT ["java", \
  "-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0", \
  "-XX:InitialRAMPercentage=50.0", \
  "-jar", "app.jar"]
```

In a 512Mi container, `MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` gives the heap approximately 384MB, leaving 128MB for metaspace, threads, code cache, and GC. In a 1Gi container, the heap gets 768MB with 256MB headroom. The **heap scales automatically** with the container size.

The JVM flag `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` — enabled by default since JDK 11 — is what makes percentage-based sizing work. It reads the cgroup memory limit from `/sys/fs/cgroup/memory/memory.limit_in_bytes` instead of looking at total host RAM. Without this flag on older JDKs, the JVM on a 64GB host would attempt to allocate a 16GB heap inside a 512Mi container.

For production deployments, inject JVM flags via `JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` in the Kubernetes deployment rather than hardcoding them in the Dockerfile. This keeps the image generic and lets you tune memory settings per environment without rebuilding.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Heap is not total JVM memory** — metaspace, thread stacks, code cache, and GC overhead can add 200-400MB beyond `-Xmx`, which is why setting heap equal to the container limit guarantees OOMKilled under load
- **`MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` scales heap to container size** — in a 512Mi container the heap gets ~384MB with 128MB headroom for non-heap regions; in a 1Gi container it scales to 768MB automatically
- **`-XX:+UseContainerSupport` reads cgroup limits** — enabled by default since JDK 11, this flag prevents the JVM from sizing heap based on total host RAM (which caused silent overcommit on older JDKs)
- **OOMKilled comes from the kernel, not the JVM** — the process receives SIGKILL with no OutOfMemoryError in logs; diagnose with `kubectl describe pod` for the OOMKilled status and `kubectl top pod` for real-time usage
- **`JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS` injects flags without rebuilding** — set it in Kubernetes env vars so the same image runs in dev, staging, and production with different memory tuning per environment

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Running a JVM inside a Docker container without explicit configuration causes the JVM to read total host memory rather than the container's memory limit, sizing its heap to 25% of the host RAM — on a 32 GB host, the JVM claims 8 GB of heap inside a container limited to 512 MB, and the kernel OOMKills it.

**Container-aware heap sizing**
- JDK 10+ respects cgroup memory limits with `-XX:+UseContainerSupport` enabled by default — the JVM reads the container limit, not host RAM, and sets initial heap to 25% of the limit
- `-XX:MaxRAMPercentage=75.0` allocates 75% of the container limit to heap — leaving 25% for non-heap memory (Metaspace, thread stacks, direct buffers, the JVM itself); using 90%+ causes frequent GC pauses as the JVM runs up against the limit before OOMKill occurs
- Verify the effective heap with `java -XX:+PrintFlagsFinal -version | grep MaxHeapSize` inside the container — compare the value to your Kubernetes resource limit to confirm they are consistent

**The direct memory trap**
- Non-heap memory is not managed by `-Xmx` — Metaspace, thread stacks (1 MB per thread by default), and direct byte buffers (NIO, gRPC, Netty) all live outside the heap limit
- A Spring Boot app under load with 50 active threads consumes 50 MB of stack alone; a Netty-based WebFlux app allocates significant direct memory; set the container limit to at least twice the configured heap to leave room for non-heap allocation
- `-XX:MaxDirectMemorySize` limits direct buffer allocation; without it, direct memory allocation is unbounded and the total process footprint can far exceed the heap limit

**Diagnostic and monitoring**
- When a container is OOMKilled, `kubectl describe pod <name>` shows `OOMKilled` in the last state with an exit code of 137 — the kill came from the container runtime, not a JVM OutOfMemoryError; the JVM had no warning
- Monitor RSS (resident set size) of the Java process with `kubectl top pod`, not just heap usage — RSS includes heap plus all non-heap memory and is what the kernel counts against the cgroup limit

questions.title: Docker Volumes: Named Volumes vs Bind Mounts
questions.direct_answer: Named volumes are managed by Docker, stored in Docker's storage area, portable across environments, and ideal for stateful data (databases, persistent uploads). Bind mounts map a host directory into the container, are tied to the host filesystem path, and ideal for development (mounting source code for hot reload). Use named volumes in production, bind mounts for local development only.

sections.title: Why Your Database Disappears Every Time You Run docker compose down
sections.content:
New Docker users discover the hard way that containers are ephemeral — stop the PostgreSQL container, start it again, and the database is empty. Every table, every row, every migration is gone because the data lived inside the container's writable layer, which is destroyed when the container is removed.

Docker provides two solutions that persist data beyond the container lifecycle: **named volumes** and **bind mounts**. They solve the same fundamental problem — making data survive container restarts — but work differently and serve different use cases. Named volumes are managed entirely by Docker, stored in Docker's internal storage area, and portable across machines. Bind mounts map a specific host directory into the container and are tied to the host's filesystem path.

The distinction matters because using the wrong type in the wrong context creates real problems. Bind mounts in production depend on host paths that may not exist, have wrong permissions, or differ between nodes. Named volumes in development lack the filesystem-watching capability that enables hot reload. Understanding when each type is appropriate prevents both data loss in production and developer friction in local workflows.

sections.title: Named Volumes vs Bind Mounts vs tmpfs — the Full Trade-off
sections.content:
Docker actually provides three mount types, each optimized for a different data lifecycle. Named volumes handle persistent production data, bind mounts enable development workflows, and tmpfs provides secure in-memory storage.

| Dimension | Named Volume | Bind Mount | tmpfs Mount |
|---|---|---|---|
| Managed by | Docker daemon | Host OS | Linux kernel (RAM) |
| Storage location | Docker's internal area | Any host path you specify | RAM only — never touches disk |
| Portability | Works on any Docker host | Depends on host path existing | Works anywhere with RAM |
| Persistence | Survives container removal | Persists on host filesystem | Lost when container stops |
| Permission model | Docker handles ownership | Inherits host file permissions | Kernel memory permissions |
| Backup approach | `docker volume` commands | Standard filesystem tools | Not applicable — ephemeral |
| Primary use case | Production databases, uploads | Dev hot-reload, config files | Secrets, temp processing files |

**tmpfs mounts** deserve attention in security-conscious environments. They store data in RAM only — nothing is written to the host filesystem or the container's writable layer. This makes them ideal for decrypted secrets, temporary processing files, or any data that should never persist to disk. The trade-off is obvious: data disappears when the container stops.

sections.title: The Decision Rule: Production Gets Volumes, Development Gets Bind Mounts
sections.content:
For **production database containers**, always use named volumes. PostgreSQL's data directory, Redis's dump files, and Elasticsearch indices belong in named volumes because Docker manages them consistently regardless of the host machine's filesystem layout.

The compose configuration for persistent PostgreSQL data demonstrates the pattern — a named volume declared at the bottom of the file and mounted into the container's data directory.

```yaml
services:
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    volumes:
      - postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data
volumes:
  postgres_data:
```

For **local development**, bind mounts enable the hot-reload workflow. Mounting your `src/` directory into the container lets Spring Boot DevTools detect file changes without rebuilding the Docker image. The container sees the same files your IDE edits in real time.

For **Spring Boot application containers** in production, the answer is usually neither — the application itself should be **stateless**. If your app writes to the local filesystem for file uploads, logs, or temporary processing, reconsider the design. Use S3 or cloud object storage for uploads, a centralized logging stack for logs, and tmpfs for temporary files. A stateless app container can be replaced, scaled, or migrated without worrying about data on a specific node.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Named volumes are Docker-managed and portable** — they persist across container restarts and work identically on any host, making them the only appropriate choice for production database data
- **Bind mounts map host directories for real-time file access** — essential for development hot-reload workflows but fragile in production because host paths and permissions vary between machines
- **`docker compose down` preserves named volumes; `down -v` destroys them** — the `-v` flag is intentional data destruction, and forgetting it (or accidentally including it) has opposite consequences depending on the situation
- **tmpfs stores sensitive data in RAM only** — decrypted secrets and temporary processing files never touch the host disk, providing a security guarantee that neither volumes nor bind mounts offer
- **Spring Boot apps should be stateless** — persistent storage belongs in database containers or cloud object storage, not inside the application container; if your app needs a volume, the architecture likely needs rethinking

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Docker provides two mechanisms for persisting data outside a container's writable layer: named volumes and bind mounts. They look similar in compose files but have completely different lifecycle characteristics.

**Named volumes — Docker-managed persistence**
- A named volume (`-v postgres_data:/var/lib/postgresql/data`) is created and managed by Docker; it persists independently of any container — `docker rm` deletes the container but not the volume
- Named volumes are stored in Docker's managed directory (usually `/var/lib/docker/volumes/`) and are not directly accessible as a regular filesystem path on the host — use `docker volume inspect` to find the mount point
- Named volumes are the right default for database data directories in development and for any data that must outlive the container; `docker compose down` preserves named volumes, `docker compose down -v` removes them explicitly

**Bind mounts — host filesystem projection**
- A bind mount (`-v /host/path:/container/path`) projects a specific host directory into the container; changes from either side are immediately visible to the other — every file the container writes appears on the host filesystem at the specified path
- Bind mounts are the right choice for development workflows where you want live reloading — mount your source directory into the container running a Spring Boot DevTools configuration so code changes reload without a container rebuild
- On macOS and Windows, bind mounts go through a filesystem sharing layer that introduces I/O overhead — file-intensive workloads (database storage, large build caches) should use named volumes instead for performance

**Security considerations**
- Bind-mounting sensitive host paths (like the Docker socket `/var/run/docker.sock`) gives the container root-equivalent access to the host — a container with the Docker socket can start privileged containers, escape the container namespace, and access any data on the host
- Named volumes do not grant host filesystem access; they are isolated to the volume's managed directory — prefer named volumes over bind mounts in production-like environments for this reason

Create a dedicated user in the Dockerfile with RUN adduser, set it with USER instruction before ENTRYPOINT, and ensure the application directory is owned by that user.
